title: Should the Weekend Bus Pilot Expand?
author: Chee Skool
prompt: Analyze both sources. Determine which argument is better supported by relevant evidence and reasoning. Use specific evidence from the sources to support your response.

sourceA.title: Expand the Pilot Carefully
sourceA.text:
A transit agency tested 20-minute Saturday service on two busy routes for four months. Average Saturday ridership on those routes increased 17 percent compared with the same months the previous year, while on-time performance remained within two percentage points of the weekday average. A rider survey of 860 passengers found that 38 percent used the added trips for work and 27 percent for medical appointments or errands. The agency estimates that expanding the schedule to four additional routes would cost $420,000 per year. It proposes a one-year expansion only on routes where weekend buses regularly reach at least 70 percent of seated capacity.

The agency also reports an important limitation. Fuel prices were lower during part of the pilot, and two large community events may have increased ridership on several weekends. For that reason, the proposal does not claim that every route needs more service. Instead, it recommends using passenger counts, missed-trip reports, and transfer connections to select the next routes. If the additional routes do not meet the ridership threshold after one year, the agency says the schedule can be reduced again.

The agency also compared the pilot routes with two similar routes that kept 30-minute Saturday service. Ridership on those comparison routes changed by less than 3 percent over the same period. Staff caution that the comparison is imperfect because neighborhoods differ, but they say it makes the 17 percent increase harder to explain only by citywide travel trends. Dispatch logs show no increase in operator overtime on the pilot routes. The proposal would require quarterly reports on ridership, missed connections, cost per passenger trip, and on-time performance.

sourceB.title: Improve Reliability Before Adding Trips
sourceB.text:
A drivers' association argues that the transit agency should first improve reliability on the current weekend schedule. Its members report that traffic near shopping districts often delays buses and causes missed transfers. The association notes that some riders may value a bus that arrives consistently more than a bus that comes more often. It recommends adding recovery time at route endpoints and assigning standby drivers during the busiest weekend periods.

The association points to 74 written rider complaints collected over six months that mention late buses or missed connections. However, the complaints cover the entire bus network, not only the two pilot routes, and the letter does not state how many total weekend trips were operated during the period. The association also does not estimate the cost of its proposed staffing changes. It agrees that some routes may eventually need more frequent service, but argues that the agency should solve reliability problems before committing to a larger expansion.

The association adds that drivers on three other weekend routes reported repeated schedule pressure near the central mall. Union records show 19 overtime extensions connected with late Saturday trips during the past quarter. The letter argues that adding trips without adjusting running time could spread the same problem. However, it does not show whether the two pilot routes had the same pressure or whether overtime came from traffic, staffing shortages, or other causes. It asks for a networkwide reliability audit before expansion.

it acknowledges confounding factors and proposes a reversible one-year test
evidence: ridership rose 17 percent while on-time performance stayed close to the weekday average
the agency limits expansion to routes meeting a capacity threshold and says service can be reduced if results are weak

modelResponse:
Both sources address the same policy question, but Source A presents the better-supported argument. Its position is stronger for two main reasons: it uses measured ridership, on-time performance, survey results, and a defined expansion threshold; and it acknowledges confounding factors and proposes a reversible one-year test. Source B raises a relevant concern, but the support behind that concern is less complete.

First, Source A is stronger because it uses measured ridership, on-time performance, survey results, and a defined expansion threshold. It reports that ridership rose 17 percent while on-time performance stayed close to the weekday average. This evidence matters because it directly addresses a central factual question behind the recommendation rather than asking the reader to accept a prediction. The evidence also fits the scope of the claim, which makes the reasoning easier to evaluate. Source B does not provide equally specific support on this point.

Source A is also stronger because it acknowledges confounding factors and proposes a reversible one-year test. It explains that the agency limits expansion to routes meeting a capacity threshold and says service can be reduced if results are weak. This matters because the source considers another important part of the decision instead of relying on a single favorable fact. Source B cites real complaints, but the complaints are network-wide and are not placed in context with total trips or costs. That concern is relevant, but the weaker source does not show that it outweighs Source A's more direct evidence or that the proposed response would fail.

Overall, Source A is better supported because its recommendation is tied to specific evidence and its reasoning stays within the limits of that evidence. Source B contributes a useful caution, but Source A gives the reader clearer grounds for judging likely results.
